## Results

### Whole-spectrum clustering and the no-peak reference

Before any normalization, the two modalities differ in absolute scale by roughly five orders of magnitude (@fig-clusters A): the median raw spectral density runs at ~$10^1-10^2$ for the intracranial recordings against ~$10^{-3} - 10^{-4}$ for the reconstructed sources. This gap reflects the difference in recording units and source-reconstruction scaling — intracranial voltage versus the inverse-solution source estimate — rather than a physical difference in power, and it is what the unit-power normalization removes so that spectral shape can be compared across modalities. All subsequent analyses are run on the normalized spectra.

#### K-means clusterization {#result-clusterisation}

In the iEEG atlas, the clustering resolved distinct, band-specific peak groups. With the 0.5-80 Hz bandpass of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial applied, it reproduced their eight-group solution: a no-peak group and seven peak groups spanning low delta, high delta, theta, alpha, low beta, high beta, and gamma. Avoiding band pass filtering reduced this to seven groups: a no-peak group and six peak clusters (two delta, one theta, two alpha, one beta clusters), with no gamma group and no low/high-beta split (@fig-clusters B). We decided to avoid bandpass filtering, as discussed in @sec-clustering.

Source-reconstructed HD-EEG produced a markedly different structure of eleven groups. Seven carried a peak in the alpha range (8-12 Hz) and differed only in amplitude, so the procedure over-segmented a single alpha-dominated continuum rather than resolving separate bands (@fig-clusters C); no distinct theta or beta cluster emerged, and the no-peak cluster was flatter than its iEEG counterpart.

We labelled each cluster by the frequency of its maximum deviation from the no-peak baseline (interpretable only where a genuine peak is present), only the δ and α HD-EEG clusters showed a clear bump above the aperiodic background. The remaining high-frequency clusters were separated by a shallower aperiodic slope and an elevated broadband tail, not by an oscillation. Where the iEEG atlas resolved oscillatory clusters from $\delta$  to $\gamma$, the HD-EEG structure reduced to alpha power and aperiodic slope (@fig-clusters).

![We show spectral clustering in iEEG and source-reconstructed HD-EEG. Panel A is the average raw (non-normalised) PSD for each modality. Panels B and C show the cluster solutions on normalised spectra: the seven iEEG clusters (B) and the eleven HD-EEG clusters (C), each including one no-peak cluster. The HD-EEG solution splits into more clusters, most separated only by the power of the alpha peak. A knee is visible in the iEEG clusters, whereas the reconstructed sources are closer to 1/f.](figures/chapter2/clusters/rawpower_and_clusters.pdf){#fig-clusters width="100%" column="page"}

Testing each region against the no-peak set across the 22 frequency intervals reproduced this contrast at regional resolution (@fig-stat-reg_dfiff). In the iEEG atlas, regions deviated from the no-peak distribution across most of the spectrum and in a regionally specific way: the alpha interval was strongest in occipital and posterior parietal cortex — up to all channels in the cuneus, ~0.86 in superior and middle occipital gyri and ~0.73 in postcentral gyrus. Parietal and frontal regions added a weaker beta component (parietal operculum ~0.56 at ~15-20 Hz; precentral up to ~0.5 at ~17-24 Hz); the highest interval reached was high-beta (24-31 Hz), while the 31.75-80 Hz gamma interval was essentially empty. The hippocampus deviated specifically in the delta range (~0.44-0.69 at 1-4 Hz). In source-reconstructed HD-EEG the deviations were dominated by a posterior alpha band (~8-13 Hz), shared across almost all regions at comparable fractions (~0.4-0.79); delta and theta were largely empty, but a parietal beta band persisted (~17-24 Hz, ~0.4-0.6) alongside a frontal high-frequency cluster (~24-80 Hz, ~0.4-0.5) that tracks the elevated broadband tail rather than a rhythm.

![Regional differences from the no-peak set across frequency intervals, for iEEG (A) and source-reconstructed HD-EEG (B). Cell coloring is the fraction of a region's channels whose relative power exceeded the no-peak distribution.](figures/chapter2/clusters/combined_regional_differences_faceted.pdf){#fig-stat-reg_dfiff width="100%" column="page"}

The same divergence appears in the lobar mean spectra overlaid on the no-peak reference (@fig-lobar-reg_dfiff). In iEEG every lobe rose above the reference with a clear alpha peak — tallest and broadest in occipital cortex — alongside additional theta and beta structure in the frontal and temporal lobes, a multimodal departure from the background. In HD-EEG each lobe instead reduced to a single sharp alpha peak, strongest in occipital and parietal lobes, with the significantly deviating frequencies confined to the alpha band and no separate theta or beta elevation.

![Lobar differences relative to the no-peak set, for iEEG (top) and source-reconstructed HD-EEG (bottom). We overlay each lobe's mean normalised spectrum on the no-peak reference; n per lobe is annotated.](figures/chapter2/clusters/combined_lobar_differences_faceted.pdf){#fig-lobar-reg_dfiff width="100%" column="page"}

#### Clustering stability and data driven intervals 

 The no-peak reference set, and the data-driven frequency intervals used for regional peak detection were sensitive to preprocessing choices and to the fitted frequency range,  small changes in the lower or upper bound altered the number of clusters and the membership and shape of the no-peak reference set. In the source-reconstructed HD-EEG data, where some configurations failed to produce a no-peak set at all.

The data-driven intervals also failed to transfer. @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial defined 22 intervals so that each held at least 4% of the total mean power in iEEG; applied to the HD-EEG spectra the same rule yielded 21 intervals and split the range above 31.75 Hz into five separate bins, where the atlas defined a single 31.75-80 Hz band. We attributed this gamma over-segmentation to the unit-power normalisation (see Discussion). Because the 4% rule did not transfer, we retained the fixed 22 intervals of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial for both modalities in all regional peak-detection tests (@fig-stat-reg_dfiff), to keep them comparable.

The clustering, the no-peak reference, and the power-based interval definition were therefore potentially unstable across reasonable preprocessing choices. We did not apply this k-means descriptor to the aperiodic-corrected (`specparam`) spectra. In the subsequent analyses we instead characterised oscillatory content with the per-band parametrised-peak descriptor, which needs neither a clustering step nor a no-peak reference and was therefore less dependent on these preprocessing choices.

###  Normalized relative-power maps before and after broadband correction

We present regional relative band power, compared across modalities, with the band- and interval-overlap metric. We read it in two states — on the uncorrected spectra in @sec-normative-uncorrected and after removing the `specparam`-estimated broadband component (@sec-normative-corrected).

#### Band-power map on uncorrected spectra {#sec-normative-uncorrected}

We mapped each region's relative band power on the uncorrected unit-power spectra, as a fraction of total power within each canonical band and interval defined in @sec-clustering. Relative band powers are compositional: the bands within a channel sum to a fixed total.  We summarize per region across channels: the group mean on the surface maps, the median in the heatmaps. We show it in two views: the band-wise spatial distribution projected onto the cortical surface (@fig-relpower-maps-uncorrected), and the full region × band matrix as heatmaps, for both band schemes and both modalities (@fig-relpower-heatmaps). The wide canonical bands carry a much larger fraction of total power than the narrower intervals, so each heatmap panel is scaled to its own maximum and colour is not comparable across panels. In both modalities the delta band carries the big fraction of total power. The clearest band-limited elevation is a posterior alpha focus, sharper in HD-EEG, and the HD-EEG heatmap additionally shows elevated power in the highest Frauscher interval (31.75-80 Hz) that the iEEG atlas lacks. 

![Group-average relative PSD per ROI, faceted by canonical band (columns) and modality (rows: iEEG top, HD-EEG source bottom). Colour is the within-band relative power (fraction of total power) on a single shared scale across all panels, so magnitude is comparable across bands and modalities — delta highest, gamma lowest. Hippocampus and amygdala have no cortical-surface geometry in the Frauscher ggsegpy atlas and are not shown.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_maps_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-maps-uncorrected}



![Median relative band power per bilateral region, before aperiodic correction, as region × band heatmaps. Modalities are stacked — iEEG (top, A-B) over HD-EEG (bottom, C-D) — with the five canonical bands (left) and the 22 @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial inspired intervals (right). Each cell is the median over a region's channels of within-band relative power (fraction of total, in [0, 1]). Colorbars are per-panel (auto-scaled), since the wide canonical bands hold far more power than the narrower bins. Rows are bilateral MICCAI regions grouped by lobe.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_heatmaps_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-heatmaps}

#### Cross-modal correlation of regional maps of uncorrected spectra

Regional relative-power maps agreed across modalities most strongly in alpha (r = 0.60) and, more weakly, in delta (r = 0.42); theta showed essentially no correspondence (r = 0.13), beta only weak agreement (r = 0.30), and gamma was anti-correlated (r = −0.29). Cross-modal preservation of the spatial pattern is therefore band-dependent: it holds in the alpha and low-frequency ranges that carry the clearest oscillatory structure and breaks down at high frequencies.

These per-band correlations are descriptive, not inferential: the regions are not independent and the relative powers are compositional (Methods), so we base formal cross-modal inference on the bootstrap overlap below and on the peak descriptors.

![Cross-modal correspondence of uncorrected relative band power. Each panel is one canonical band; each point is one bilateral MICCAI region, with source HD-EEG relative power on the x-axis and the iEEG atlas on the y-axis. Points are coloured by lobe, the solid line is the per-band OLS fit, and the dashed line marks identity (y = x). Strip labels give the per-band Pearson correlation.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_scatter_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-scatter-uncorrected}

#### Bootstrapped cross-modal overlap on uncorrected spectra

To compare directly with the clustering analysis, we recomputed the overlap in the same heatmap display (@fig-overlap-pair-uncorrected). The overlap is strongest in the delta and alpha bands, with beta present in some regions. Cells are masked where the bootstrap 95% CI of the overlap includes zero, and a contrast dot marks cells where a reliable overlap sits on a flat residual — a reliable agreement with no significant rhythm in either modality, which matters for the presence-conditioned analysis below.

![Cross-modal spectral overlap between the iEEG atlas and source-reconstructed HD-EEG mapped onto the cortex, one panel per canonical band (left hemisphere, lateral and medial views), computed on uncorrected relative-power PSDs. Each bilateral MICCAI region is coloured by its band-averaged Afnan overlap on a fixed 0-1 scale — the metric is already bounded, so colour is comparable across bands and across regions; the strip reports the per-band mean overlap across regions. Hippocampus and amygdala have no cortical-surface geometry in the Frauscher ggsegpy atlas and are not shown.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_maps_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-overlap-maps-uncorrected}



![Uncorrected cross-modal overlap. A) five canonical EEG bands B) the 22 intervals defined in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial. Both panels are masked (grey) where the bootstrap 95% CI of the overlap includes 0 and carry a contrast dot where a reliable overlap sits on a flat residual (no significant rhythm in either modality — spurious agreement).](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_pair_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-overlap-pair-uncorrected}



#### Aperiodic-removed band power {#sec-normative-corrected}

We now repeat the same three views on the periodic part of the spectrum. Each channel is fit with specparam in its BIC-selected aperiodic mode (knee for iEEG, fixed for HD-EEG), and the fitted aperiodic component is subtracted from the normalised spectrum, so the per-band value is the channel's oscillatory power as a fraction of total power — on the same footing as the uncorrected relative band power above.

The fitted aperiodic parameters (@tbl-aperiodic-params) summarise each modality's $1/f$ background. Offset and exponent are mean ± sd across channels; the knee is reported as the knee _frequency_ ($\text{knee}^{1/\chi}$, in Hz) as median [IQR], since the raw knee parameter is heavy-tailed (a few channels push the knee out of band).

| modality | n channels | offset | exponent | knee freq (Hz) | R² (mean) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iEEG (knee) | 1772 | 5.096 ± 1.570 | 3.392 ± 0.884 | 11.23 [7.76, 15.92] | 0.982 |
| HD-EEG (fixed) | 1444 | -2.787 ± 0.577 | 0.944 ± 0.325 | — | 0.908 |

: Fitted aperiodic parameters per modality. {#tbl-aperiodic-params}

The two modalities differ sharply in fit quality. In the iEEG atlas the knee model captured the background well and consistently (mean R² 0.98, only 4/1772 channels below 0.90). The fixed model on the source-reconstructed HD-EEG channels fit less well and far more variably (mean R² 0.91; 376/1444, 26%, below 0.90), with a much lower offset and a far shallower exponent (≈0.94 vs 3.39); mean absolute error was nonetheless comparable (0.087 vs 0.073 in log₁₀ power). The poorer, more dispersed HD-EEG fits and shallow exponent indicate that the HD-EEG aperiodic estimate — and hence its oscillatory residual — is less reliable than the iEEG one.

Removing the aperiodic background isolates the rhythmic peaks from the $1/f$ tail, so the correspondence is no longer inflated (or, in gamma, depressed) by the steepness of the background. The closure constraint still applies — the linear residual is normalised to total power — so these per-band correlations remain descriptiv


#### Band-power map on corrected spectra

We repeat the two map views on the oscillatory residual — the normalised spectrum with its fitted aperiodic component removed — so each value is a region's within-band oscillatory power as a fraction of total power, summarised across channels as the group mean on the surface maps (@fig-relpower-maps-corrected) and the median in the heatmaps (@fig-relpower-heatmaps-corrected). As before, each heatmap panel is scaled to its own maximum, so colour is not comparable across panels, and the sub-1 Hz Frauscher interval is blank because the residual is defined only on the 1-80 Hz fit grid. 

Removing the $1/f$ background leaves two dominant residuals — delta and alpha — while the gamma fraction collapses to near zero in both modalities. Alpha is posterior (occipital and parietal) in both, and markedly stronger and broader in HD-EEG, where it spreads across most regions. Delta, by contrast, is prominently widespread  in iEEG, strongest over frontal and temporal cortex — but weaker in HD-EEG. EEG further retains a moderate theta residual over temporal cortex and a beta residual over sensorimotor and parietal cortex, whereas HD-EEG largely lacks theta and has strongly reduced beta. iEEG residual stays multimodal where HD-EEG reduces to alpha.

Colour is the within-band oscillatory residual (fraction of total power) on a single shared scale across all panels, so magnitude is comparable across bands and modalities — alpha highest, gamma near zero. Hippocampus and amygdala have no cortical-surface geometry in the Frauscher ggsegpy atlas and are not shown.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_maps_corrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-maps-corrected}

![Median oscillatory band power per bilateral region after specparam aperiodic correction — the aperiodic-removed twin of @fig-relpower-heatmaps, same stacked layout: iEEG (top, A-B) over HD-EEG (bottom, C-D), canonical bands (left) and the 22 Frauscher intervals (right). Each cell is the median across the region's channels of the within-band oscillatory residual (a fraction of total power, so directly comparable to the uncorrected relative band power); each panel has its own colorbar auto-scaled to its maximum. The sub-1 Hz Frauscher interval is blank (the residual is defined on the 1-80 Hz fit grid). Rows are bilateral MICCAI regions grouped by lobe, with lobe-coloured labels.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_heatmaps_corrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-heatmaps-corrected}


#### Cross-modal correlation of regional maps of corrected spectra

Across the 38 bilateral regions the oscillatory-residual maps corresponded most strongly in the alpha band (r = 0.65), with weaker positive correspondence in delta (r = 0.35), theta (r = 0.24) and beta (r = 0.26), and a negative correlation in gamma (r = −0.26; @fig-relpower-scatter-corrected). In alpha the occipital and parietal regions carry the largest residual in both modalities.

Each panel is one canonical band; each point is one bilateral MICCAI region, source HD-EEG oscillatory residual on x and the iEEG atlas on y. Points are coloured by lobe, the solid line is the per-band OLS fit, and the dashed line marks identity (y = x). The residual is the specparam linear oscillatory power (band fraction of total) with the BIC-selected aperiodic component removed.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_scatter_corrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-scatter-corrected}

#### Bootstrapped cross-modal overlap on corrected spectra

Under the confidence-interval masking, reliable overlap of the aperiodic-removed spectra concentrated in delta and alpha across most regions, with beta in a subset; on the 22 Frauscher intervals most higher-frequency cells were masked (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected).

In the residual spectra the band-overlap was strongest in delta and alpha across most regions, present in beta in a subset, and weakest in gamma (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected, A); on the 22 Frauscher intervals the reliable cells concentrated in the low-frequency and alpha intervals, with much of the higher-frequency range masked where the bootstrap interval included zero (B).

Both panels are masked (grey) where the bootstrap 95% CI of the overlap includes 0 and carry a contrast dot where a reliable overlap sits on a flat residual (no significant rhythm in either modality — spurious agreement).](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_pair_corrected.pdf){#fig-overlap-pair-corrected}

 Conditioning instead on rhythm presence, the cells where both modalities carried a genuine rhythm were concentrated in alpha — high overlap in posterior regions — with some delta, whereas many beta and gamma cells were marked where the iEEG atlas carried a rhythm that source HD-EEG did not recover, most often in frontal and temporal regions (@fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair).

 This uses the same subject-clustered bootstrap of the oscillatory-residual band power (95% CI > 0), referenced to the iEEG atlas, to drive the canonical-band overlap shown in @fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair.

Same renderer as the confidence-interval pair (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected); only the masking rule differs (presence rather than the overlap's confidence interval), and the band scheme differs between panels.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_pair_corrected_presencegated.pdf){#fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair}

#### lKg vs linear aperiodic correction

Removing the aperiodic component changes the cross-modal picture, and the change depends on how the oscillatory residual is defined. We computed the per-lobe oscillatory spectrum in 2 Hz bins under four extractors — the detrended residual and the modelled (specparam-peak) power, each in a log and a linear form — and compared modalities with a subject-clustered bootstrap (per-lobe mean ± 95% CI, @fig-residual-state)

![Per-lobe oscillatory power in 2 Hz bins (subject-clustered bootstrap mean ± 95% CI), for the four extractors (rows: detrended residual / modelled, in log and linear form) and the two modalities (columns). Lines coloured by lobe.](figures/chapter2/peaks/lobe_oscillatory_state_bootstrap.pdf){#fig-residual-state width="100%" column="page"}


### Directly modelled specparam peaks

Having modelled the oscillatory peaks explicitly, we characterize them by three properties: where they sit (centre frequency), how often they occur (prevalence), and how strong they are (modelled amplitude).

#### Peak centre frequency

 We examined the fitted centre frequencies directly. The HD-EEG centre-frequency distribution is a sharp alpha mode at ~10 Hz, sitting squarely against the 8 and 13 Hz band edges, whereas iEEG peaks are broadly distributed with an additional high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz (@fig-centre-freq). The per-region dominant peak frequency — the centre frequency of the single highest-amplitude peak — is alpha-locked across almost all regions in HD-EEG but scatters into beta and gamma for several frontal and insular regions in iEEG — most extremely the inferior frontal gyrus and posterior cingulate (@fig-dominant-dumbbell). The full per-region distribution of peak frequencies confirms a narrow posterior alpha ridge in HD against broader, multimodal iEEG ridges (@fig-region-ridges).

![Distribution of fitted peak centre frequencies per modality, against the canonical band edges (dashed). HD-EEG shows a single sharp ~10 Hz alpha mode; iEEG is broad with a high-gamma cluster.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_centre_frequency_distribution.pdf){#fig-centre-freq width="80%"}

![Dominant peak frequency per region: the centre frequency of the highest-amplitude peak, connecting iEEG (blue) and source HD-EEG (red) for each region. Regions follow the lobe order and colouring of the heatmaps.](figures/chapter2/peaks/dominant_frequency_dumbbell.pdf){#fig-dominant-dumbbell width="70%"}

![Per-region distribution of peak centre frequencies (histogram ridgeline, normalised per region), filled by lobe. HD-EEG (right) is a narrow posterior alpha ridge; iEEG (left) is broader and multimodal.](figures/chapter2/peaks/region_frequency_ridges.pdf){#fig-region-ridges width="100%" column="page"}

Pooling all regions, the joint distribution of peak amplitude and centre frequency (@fig-size-freq) shows the same contrast: HD-EEG peaks form one dense high-amplitude alpha mode at ~10 Hz with a sparse low-amplitude tail above it, whereas iEEG peaks spread along the frequency axis at moderate amplitude, with a distinct beta/low-gamma body and a high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz.

![Peak size (amplitude) vs centre frequency, binned density per modality (all regions pooled). HD-EEG is a single high-amplitude alpha mode; iEEG is spread across frequency with a high-gamma cluster.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_size_vs_frequency.pdf){#fig-size-freq width="100%" column="page"}

Jointly resolving peak amplitude and centre frequency per lobe (@fig-size-freq-lobe) confirms that the two descriptors are not redundant. In HD-EEG the per-channel peak density concentrates into a single tall alpha column in occipital and parietal lobes — high amplitude at ~10 Hz — and thins sharply elsewhere. In iEEG the density is spread along the frequency axis at moderate amplitude, with frontal and temporal lobes carrying beta and low-gamma peaks that have no HD-EEG counterpart. Normalising to peaks per channel makes the lobes comparable despite their different channel counts, and shows the cross-modal divergence is one of *where in the spectrum* rhythms occur, not merely how strong they are.

![Peak size (amplitude) vs centre frequency, binned density per lobe (rows) and modality (columns), normalised to peaks per channel so lobes of different size are comparable. HD-EEG concentrates in a posterior alpha column; iEEG spreads across frequency, with frontal/temporal beta-gamma.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_size_vs_frequency_by_lobe.pdf){#fig-size-freq-lobe width="100%" column="page"}

#### Peaks prevalence

Once oscillations are modelled explicitly, peak prevalence — the fraction of a region's channels carrying at least one fitted peak in a band — diverges sharply between modalities (@fig-peak-prevalence). Source HD-EEG is dominated by alpha: mean prevalence across regions is 0.63 in alpha but only 0.11 in theta, 0.05 in gamma and 0.01 in delta. The iEEG atlas is broader, with substantial beta (0.40), gamma (0.26) and alpha (0.24) prevalence. The difference map (HD − iEEG) is strongly positive in alpha — HD detects alpha peaks far more often, especially in posterior regions — and negative across beta and gamma, where iEEG detects high-frequency peaks that the source fit does not recover.

Cross-modal agreement of the regional prevalence *pattern* (Spearman across the 38 bilateral regions) is confined to the low and mid bands: alpha $\rho = 0.60$ and beta $\rho = 0.47$, against delta $\rho = 0.04$, theta $\rho = -0.07$ and gamma $\rho = -0.25$ (@fig-prevalence-scatter). In alpha the points sit above the identity line — HD detects alpha in more regions than iEEG — yet the two modalities still rank regions consistently. This mirrors the uncorrected relative-band-power result (alpha strongest, gamma anti-correlated), now with the aperiodic background modelled out rather than carried in the power.

Because modelled power exists only where a peak is fitted, prevalence is also the peak-detection rate and must be read alongside the amplitude and centre-frequency descriptors. Mean peaks per channel were similar across modalities (iEEG 1.45, HD 1.37 under the main settings), but 99.7% of iEEG channels passed the $R^2 > 0.9$ screen against only 74.0% of HD channels, with the missing HD peaks concentrated in the high-frequency bands where the source spectrum is flattest.

![Per-band peak prevalence by region and modality (specparam peaks, BIC-selected aperiodic mode). Regions are grouped by lobe; cell colour is the fraction of a region's channels with at least one peak in the band.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_prevalence_heatmap.pdf){#fig-peak-prevalence width="100%" column="page"}

![Prevalence difference (source HD-EEG − iEEG atlas). Blue: HD detects the band more often (strong in alpha); red: iEEG more often (beta/gamma).](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_prevalence_difference_heatmap.pdf){#fig-prevalence-diff width="70%"}


#### Modelled power

The amplitude of the highest peak per band (median across the channels that carry a peak) is not redundant with prevalence. In HD-EEG the largest modelled power sits in posterior alpha, matching the prevalence pattern. In iEEG, by contrast, amplitude is spread across bands and regions with no single dominant band — the tallest peaks fall in scattered delta, theta and alpha regions rather than tracking the broad beta detection of the prevalence map (@fig-modelled-power).

![Modelled band power by region and modality: median amplitude (log-power height above the aperiodic component) of the highest peak in each band, over channels with a detected peak.](figures/chapter2/peaks/modelled_power_heatmap.pdf){#fig-modelled-power width="100%" column="page"}
